summary: States the requirements for converting a permanent connection into a soft permanent connection, and the reverse, in a GMPLS network without disturbing the traffic it carries. From a carrier viewpoint, this changes who owns and controls the connection.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5493 sets out what has to happen when a carrier takes a working transport connection and moves it from being controlled by the network management system to being controlled by the signalling protocols. The traffic on it must not notice.

subtitle: Moving a live transport connection from management control to signalling control, without dropping traffic.

tldr.problem: A carrier that introduces a GMPLS control plane into an existing transport network has connections that are already in service and owned by the management system, and it wants some of them under signalling control.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines permanent, switched and soft permanent connections in terms of which planes hold state and own resources, and sets out the requirements for a conversion procedure that changes ownership hop by hop.
tldr.outcome: The requirements insist that the data plane path and resources stay exactly as they are, that no user traffic is disturbed, and that a failed conversion leaves ownership unchanged.

today: RFC 5493 is an Informational document and is not listed as obsoleted or updated. It states requirements for a conversion procedure rather than specifying a protocol, and it builds on the GMPLS architecture described in RFC 3945.

sections.title: Introduction: Permanent, Switched and Soft Permanent Connections
sections.content:
In a typical traditional transport network, data plane connections between two end points are controlled by a Network Management System operating within the management plane. The management system and plane are the owner of such transport connections and are responsible for their setup, teardown and maintenance. Connections of this type, initiated and managed by the management plane, are known as permanent connections.

When the setup, teardown and maintenance of connections are achieved by a signalling protocol owned by the control plane, such connections are known as switched connections. In many deployments a hybrid connection type is used: a soft permanent connection is a combination of a permanent connection segment on the source user to network side, a permanent connection segment on the destination user to network side, and a switched connection segment within the core network. The permanent parts of the soft permanent connection are owned by the management plane and the switched parts by the control plane.

Some aspects of a control-plane-initiated connection must be capable of being queried or controlled by the management plane, and those aspects should be independent of how the connection was established.

The point of the document is that turning a permanent connection into a soft permanent connection or a switched connection, and back again, without affecting the data plane traffic being carried, is a valuable option for a carrier. Such an operation can be seen as a way of transferring the ownership and control of an existing and in-use data plane connection between the management plane and the control plane, leaving its data plane state untouched. The document sets out the requirements for those procedures within a GMPLS network.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to run a transport circuit. A network management system can build and maintain it, or the signalling protocols can. A third form mixes the two: the ends are managed and the middle is signalled. This document is about moving a live circuit from one of these forms to another without the customer noticing.

sections.title: What a Label Switched Path Means in Each Plane
sections.content:
A Label Switched Path has different semantics depending on the plane in which the term is used. In the data plane, an LSP indicates the data plane forwarding path: it defines the forwarding or switching operations at each network entity, and it is the sequence of data plane resources, links, labels and cross-connects, that achieves end-to-end data transport. In the management plane, an LSP is the management plane state information, such as the connection attributes and the path information, associated with and necessary for the creation and maintenance of a data plane connection. In the control plane, an LSP is the control plane state information, such as the RSVP-TE path and reservation state, associated with and necessary for the creation and maintenance of a data plane connection.

A permanent connection has an LSP presence in the data plane and in the management plane. A switched connection has an LSP presence in the data plane and in the control plane. A soft permanent connection has an LSP presence in the data plane for its entire length, but a management plane presence for part of its length and a control plane presence for part of its length. When the document discusses conversion between the management plane and the control plane, it focuses on the conversion of the control plane state information and the management plane state information.
sections.plainLanguage: The same circuit has three descriptions. One is the path the traffic actually takes. The other two are the paperwork: what the management system believes, and what the signalling protocol believes. A conversion changes the paperwork and leaves the traffic alone.

sections.title: Resource Ownership and Setting Up a GMPLS-Controlled Network
sections.content:
GMPLS defines a control plane architecture for transport networks, including routing and signalling protocols for creating and maintaining label switched paths in networks whose data plane is based on different technologies, such as Time Division Multiplexing at the ODUk level and Wavelength Division Multiplexing at the OCh level.

A resource used by an LSP is said to be owned by the plane that was used to set up the LSP through that part of the network. All the resources used by a permanent connection are therefore owned by the management plane, and all the resources used by a switched connection are owned by the control plane. The resources used by a soft permanent connection are divided between the management plane, for the resources of the permanent segments at the edge of the network, and the control plane, for the resources of the switched segments in the middle.

How the resources available for ownership are divided between the two planes is an architectural issue. A carrier may decide to pre-partition the resources at a network entity so that LSPs under management plane control use one set of resources and LSPs under control plane control use another. Other carriers may make the distinction resource by resource as LSPs are established. Even when a resource is owned by the control plane, the management plane will usually have a controlling interest in it, for example because management commands must be able to put a laser out of service for basic safety reasons.

Implementing a new network with a GMPLS control plane can be considered a green field deployment, but in many cases it is desirable to introduce a GMPLS control plane into an existing transport network already populated with permanent connections under management plane control. In that mixed scenario, permanent connections owned by the management plane and switched connections owned by the control plane have to coexist within the network. It is also desirable to transfer the control of connections from the management plane to the control plane so that connections originally under the control of a network management system come under the control of the GMPLS protocols, and where such connections are in service the conversion must be performed in a way that does not affect traffic.

Since attempts to move an LSP under GMPLS control might fail for reasons outside the scope of the document, it is also highly desirable to have a mechanism to convert the control of an LSP back to the management plane. A permanent connection may be converted to a switched connection or to a soft permanent connection, and a soft permanent connection may be converted to a switched connection as well, so the reverse mappings may also be needed.

Conversion to and from the control and management planes occurs in management information bases or in information stored on the device, such as the cross-connect, label assignment and label stacking, and is identified as either initiated by a specific control protocol or by manual operation through a network management system. When converting, this hop-level owner information needs to be completed for all hops. If the conversion cannot be done for all hops, then it must be done for no hops, the state of the hop-level information must be restored to what it was before the attempt, and an error condition must be reported to the management system.

In either case of conversion, the management plane shall initiate the change. When converting from a permanent connection to a switched connection, the management system must indicate to each hop that a control protocol is now to be used, and then configure the data needed by the control protocol at the connection endpoints. When converting from a switched connection to a permanent connection, the management plane must change the owner of each hop, and then the instance in the control plane must be removed without affecting the data plane. The case where the control plane and or the management plane fail at one or more nodes during the conversion procedure must be handled in the solution. If the network is viewed as the database of record, including data, control and management plane elements, then a solution with procedures similar to those of a two-phase database commit process may be needed, to ensure integrity and to support the need to revert to the state prior to the conversion attempt.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece of the network, each link, label and cross-connect, belongs to whichever plane set it up. The management plane may still have a say over a signalled piece, because it has to be able to shut a laser down for safety. The conversion itself is done hop by hop, and the rule is all or nothing: if one hop cannot be converted, none of them may be, the records are put back as they were, and the management system is told it failed.

sections.title: Typical Use Cases
sections.content:
A typical scenario where a permanent connection to switched connection, or to soft permanent connection, procedure is useful is at the initial stage of control plane deployment in an existing network. All the network connections, possibly carrying traffic, are already set up as permanent connections and owned by the management plane.

At a later stage, when the network is partially controlled by the management plane and partially by the control plane, with permanent connections and switched or soft permanent connections coexisting, and it is desired to extend the control plane, a permanent connection to switched connection procedure can be used to transfer a permanent connection or a soft permanent connection to a switched connection. In both cases a connection set up and owned by the management plane needs to be transferred to control plane control, and if the connection is carrying traffic, its control transfer has to be done without any disruption to the data plane traffic.

The main need for a switched connection to permanent connection conversion is to give an operator the capability of undoing the action of the above conversion. The document stresses that such a conversion needs to be achieved without any effect on the associated data plane state, so that the connection continues to be operational and to carry traffic during the transition. The back-out procedure is not specified as mandatory in the document, but it is described as a highly desirable function.
sections.plainLanguage: The expected use is the early stage of a migration: a network that is being partly converted to signalling control. Each circuit is handed over one at a time, and the operator needs a way to take one back if the conversion goes wrong.

sections.title: The Requirements
sections.content:
The data plane LSP MUST stay in place throughout the whole control transfer process: it MUST follow the same path through the network and MUST use the same network resources. The transfer process MUST NOT cause any disruption of user traffic flowing over the LSP whose control is being transferred, or over any other LSP in the network, and conversion in either direction SHALL occur without generating alarms towards the end users or the network management system.

It MUST be possible to transfer the ownership of an LSP from the management plane to the control plane, and it SHOULD be possible to transfer ownership from the control plane back to the management plane. It MUST be assured that the state of the LSP is synchronized among all nodes traversed by it before the conversion is considered complete. It MUST be possible to segment an LSP such that it can be converted to or from a soft permanent connection.

It MUST be possible for a transfer from one plane to the other to fail in a non-destructive way, leaving the ownership unchanged and without impacting traffic. If issues arise during the transfer procedure causing an unsuccessful or unexpected result, it MUST be assured that traffic over the data plane is not affected, and that the LSP status is consistent in all the network nodes involved in the procedure. The second point assures that even in case of some failure during the transfer, the state of the affected LSP is brought back to the initial one and is fully under the control of the owning entity.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are strict on purpose. The path must not change, the traffic must not blink, no alarm may reach the customer, and every node must agree on the state before the job is called done. If anything goes wrong halfway, the connection must end up exactly as it started, still owned by whoever owned it, still carrying traffic.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Allowing the control of an LSP to be taken away from a plane introduces a possible way in which services may be disrupted by malicious intervention. A solution to the requirements in the document will use the security mechanisms supported by the management plane and the GMPLS control plane protocols, and no new security requirements beyond the general requirements of the GMPLS architecture are introduced. It is expected that solution documents will include an analysis of the security issues introduced by any new protocol extensions.

The management plane interactions MUST be supported through protocols that can offer adequate security mechanisms to secure the configuration and protect the operation of the managed devices. Those mechanisms MUST include at least cryptographic security and the ability to ensure that the entity given access to configuration parameters is properly configured to give access only to those principals that have legitimate rights to read, create, change or delete the parameters. The IETF standard management protocols Netconf and SNMPv3 offer these mechanisms. Implementations may also support policy components to determine whether individual LSPs may be transferred between planes.
sections.plainLanguage: Handing a circuit over to another system is a chance for someone to interfere, so the management channel has to be protected with cryptography and has to check who is allowed to change what. The document points at two standard management protocols that already do this.

viz.caption: WHERE EACH KIND OF CONNECTION HAS ITS STATE
THE SEVEN REQUIREMENTS FOR A CONVERSION PROCEDURE

items.title: Data plane consistency
items.text: The data plane path must stay in place, follow the same route and use the same resources.

items.title: No disruption of user traffic
items.text: No traffic on the transferred path or any other path may be disrupted, and no alarm may reach the users or the management system.

items.title: Management plane to control plane
items.text: It must be possible to transfer ownership of a path from the management plane to the control plane.

items.title: Control plane to management plane
items.text: It should be possible to transfer ownership back to the management plane.

items.title: Synchronization among nodes
items.text: The state must be synchronized across all the nodes the path traverses before the conversion counts as complete.

items.title: Soft permanent connections
items.text: It must be possible to segment a path so it can be converted to or from a soft permanent connection.

items.title: Failure of transfer
items.text: A failed transfer must leave ownership unchanged, leave traffic unaffected, and put the state back as it was.
